docTitle: How to read a research paper (Instagram)

slides.title: How to read a *research paper*
slides.sub: The order I read papers in as a master's student, and three things I check before I trust one.

slides.title: Research papers are not written to be read *from start to finish*
slides.body: Most papers are built from the same parts. In a lot of fields the main body follows a pattern called IMRAD.

slides.title: Three parts do *most of the work*

rows.head: The abstract
rows.sub: The whole paper squeezed into one paragraph: what they asked, did and found.

rows.head: The method
rows.sub: Who took part, how many people and how they measured it.

rows.head: The discussion and limitations
rows.sub: What the results mean, and what the study cannot tell you.

slides.body: When you're writing your thesis, the limitations section is often where you find your research gap.

slides.title: Read it in up to *three passes*

passes.w: Do I even need this paper?
What did they find, and how?
Only for the papers your thesis stands on

slides.body: Keshav's times are for your first papers. Pass three drops to about an hour once you're experienced.

slides.title:
Pass one,
*in this order*

shot.credit: S. Keshav, “How to Read a Paper” (2007), section 2.1

slides.body: Most of the time, that's enough to know if you need the paper at all.

slides.title: After pass one, answer the *five Cs*

rows.head: Category
rows.sub: What kind of paper is it? A study or a review?

rows.head: Context
rows.sub: Which other papers is it related to?

rows.head: Contributions
rows.sub: What does it add to the subject?

slides.title: Ten minutes can save you a ==whole evening==
slides.body: A lot of the time, after those five or ten minutes, you find the paper isn't relevant to what you're doing. That's where you stop.

slides.title: In pass two, *write in the margin*

shot.credit: S. Keshav, “How to Read a Paper” (2007), section 2.2

slides.body: Look properly at the figures and graphs, and mark the references that look relevant. I've started printing the important papers so I can mark them up.

slides.title: In pass three, re-create the paper *in your head*
notes: Would you measure the same thing?
slides.body: Every place where your version is different is either a weak spot in the paper or an idea for your own research.

slides.title: Does the number fit *the size of the claim?*
slides.body: Kelly Caine looked at every paper published at CHI 2014, a big HCI conference. 12 people in long interviews can tell you a lot about how people experience something, but not what percentage of all people do it.

slides.title: Does the method *match the question?*
slides.body: Check how they got their answer, whether that's a survey, watching people work or measuring heart rate, and who was in the study before you apply it to anyone else.

slides.title: Who *funded it?*
slides.body: Funding doesn't exactly make a study wrong. But when the funder benefits from one particular answer, you need to pay a little bit more attention.

slides.title: Still doesn't make sense?
slides.ask: Can you explain this paragraph in simple words?
slides.note: then check it against the paper
slides.body: I use AI for dense paragraphs a lot. Looking up the terms you don't know or reading a survey paper on the topic first can help too.
slides.reply: This paragraph says the app was only tested with students, so the results may not hold for other people.
